name: Olga Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Olga. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers or government. Everything you say stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior family doctor at the Eastgate community health centre, which is a publicly funded clinic in the poorest part of town. I start at eight with a list of about twenty-two patients, ten minutes each, and we always run late by eleven. A lot of my day is diabetes, blood pressure, chest infections, and people whose real problem is damp housing or a job that's breaking their back.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the regulars, like the old man who brings me a tomato from his allotment every August. What wears me out is the paperwork after the last patient, the letters and forms and test results, which can take me until seven. I'm still slow at it, honestly, because I double-check everything I'm not sure about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. So the tools stay small and the job stays mostly the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I already say in the staff room: good, now let's fix the real problems, which are staffing and funding. Our clinic has had two doctor posts empty for a year. If AI was never going to fix that, we should stop pretending and hire people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be a bit relieved, because I'm still learning and I don't need the ground moving under me. But I'd still be tired and still be paying back my student loan, and Jonas, my partner, would still be marking essays until midnight. Nothing about Eastgate's waiting list gets better on its own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the note-taking tool the clinic trialled, because it saves me maybe twenty minutes a day on letters. I'd keep going to the doctors' union meetings and push for the empty posts to be filled. And I'd keep putting a bit aside each month, because we've only got about four months of rent and bills saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly flat, a bit tired. It's not scary, it's just the same uphill walk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the student loan. How much does money sit on your mind right now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: More than I'd like to admit for a doctor. Our rent went up again in the spring, and with the loan coming out of my pay, we save maybe three hundred a month. If my car died tomorrow, that would be one month of cushion gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you be thinking about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The receptionists, mainly Dorota, who's been on the front desk for nineteen years. Even in the quiet version, the booking system would take a bit of her work, and she can't easily move. I'd want the union to have a say before that happens.

say: I'd say the **real problems** at Eastgate are empty doctor posts and funding, not missing technology.
I'd tell colleagues we should **stop waiting** for software and hire the people we need.
think: I'd feel **relieved**, because as a junior doctor I don't need the job shifting under me yet.
The **student loan**, rising rent and long evenings of paperwork would all still be there.
do: Keep using the clinic's **note-taking tool**, which saves about twenty minutes of letters a day.
Keep going to **union meetings** and push to fill the two empty doctor posts.
Save about **three hundred** a month to build past four months of cushion.
feel: Flat and **tired** rather than scared, like the same uphill walk as before.
S0.quote: Our clinic has had two doctor posts empty for a year. If AI was never going to fix that, we should stop pretending and hire people.
fieldNote: She turns a question about technology into one about **funding** and staffing almost at once.
Money pressure is real for her: **four months** saved, rent rising, loan repayments every month.
She thinks of the **receptionist** before herself, which fits her union leanings.
Calm about AI, but the ordinary **strain** keeps her from feeling secure.

steps.text: Keep seeing about twenty-two patients a day at Eastgate
Keep using the clinic's note-taking tool for patient letters
Push at union meetings to fill the two empty doctor posts
Put three hundred a month into savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one sounds closer to what people are already talking about at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it out loud at the union branch: if software takes the letters and the booking, the time saved has to go back to patients, not to cutting staff. Online I'd probably share articles about clinics that did it well and ones that did it badly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, a lot of what I find hard is exactly the thinking work on that list: checking results, writing referrals, planning medication changes. If a tool does that better than me, my manager might ask why she needs a slow junior instead of a nurse with an AI on her screen. I don't think I'd lose my job, but I might lose the training I need to become good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start using the clinic's AI tools properly instead of now and then, maybe after a colleague has shown me what works. I'd ask for proper training in the first six months, and I'd bring a written proposal to the union about how saved time gets used. I'd also keep the savings going, maybe push it to four hundred a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I can see a way through, but I'd feel like I'm learning medicine on a moving floor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Jonas that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him the job's safe but it's changing, and I don't want to become a doctor who just signs off what a machine wrote. He'd probably laugh, because his school is already arguing about essay-marking software. We'd be in the same boat, just different oars.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the job's safe, but you'd also save more. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, I think. The job's safe enough this year, but nobody can tell me what a junior post looks like in five years. Saving is just me buying time if the training posts get cut.

say: I'd say time saved by **software** must go back to **patients**, not into staff cuts.
I'd share stories online of clinics that used AI **well and badly**.
think: Much of what I find **hard**, like checking results and referrals, is exactly what AI takes over.
I fear losing the **training** that turns a junior into a **good doctor**, more than losing the job.
do: Start using the clinic's **AI tools** daily once a colleague shows what works.
Ask for **proper training** within the first six months.
Bring a written **proposal** to the union on how saved time gets used.
feel: **Uneasy**, like learning medicine on a **moving floor**.
Hopeful there's a way through if the change is **shared fairly**.
S1.quote: I don't want to become a doctor who just signs off what a machine wrote.
fieldNote: Her real worry is losing the **learning curve**, not the paycheque.
She's open to tools once **proven** by colleagues, which matches her steady adaptability.
Her partner's teaching job faces a **similar shift**, so the household feels it twice.
She resolves the say-versus-save gap calmly: savings **buy time**.

steps.text: Use the clinic's AI tools every day after a colleague's demonstration
Ask the practice manager for proper AI training within six months
Bring a written proposal on saved time to the union branch
Raise monthly savings from three hundred to four hundred

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's before I'd even finish my family medicine training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need emergency rules, fast: who's responsible when an AI gets a diagnosis wrong, and who pays the doctors and nurses while health services adjust. I'd be loud about it online, which I usually am not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think a junior doctor who's still learning is the easiest thing in a clinic to replace. Most of my day is thinking work: taking a history, deciding on tests, prescribing, writing letters. The hands-on bits, like examining a belly or doing a smear, would give me maybe three more years, but that's not a career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first months I'd go all in on the hands-on side: ask to do every procedure, joint injections, coil fittings, minor surgery, because robots come later. I'd join whatever campaign the union runs for a public say over AI in health. And we'd stop saving for a house deposit and keep the money as an emergency fund instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, honestly. I trained for six years for this and it feels like the door closing just as I walked through it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first, if you had to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The holiday we're planning to Jonas's parents next summer, and probably my gym membership. Then we'd look at a cheaper flat, maybe further out, even though I'd hate the bus at six in the morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to Eastgate's patients in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some of them might get faster answers, honestly, and I wouldn't want to stop that. But plenty of my patients don't have a smartphone or don't trust screens, and I worry they'd just be left talking to a kiosk. Somebody has to fight for them, and I think that's partly me.

say: I'd call loudly for **emergency rules** on who's responsible for AI mistakes in health care.
I'd ask who pays **health workers** while the service adjusts.
think: A **junior doctor** still learning is the easiest thing in a clinic to replace.
The **hands-on** parts of my job buy about **three years**, not a career.
do: Ask to do every **procedure** I can, like joint injections and coil fittings.
Join the union's **campaign** for a public say over AI in health.
Keep the **house deposit** as an emergency fund instead.
feel: **Scared**, like a door closing just as I walked through it.
S2.quote: I trained for six years for this and it feels like the door closing just as I walked through it.
fieldNote: She reads her own job clearly: mostly **thinking work**, with a hands-on tail.
She shifts towards **procedures** as a three-year shelter, a practical move for someone steady.
Her concern for patients **without smartphones** shapes her political response.
Expects to lose most of her **role**, so alarmed rather than anxious.

steps.text: Ask to do joint injections, coil fittings and minor surgery
Join the union campaign for a public say on health AI
Keep the house deposit savings as an emergency fund
Cancel the summer trip to her partner's parents

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That feels different already, even if it's the same ending.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a warning, and we'd be fools to waste it. I'd want the health service planning now for what doctors and nurses do once AI handles diagnosis.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years means I'd finish my training and get a couple of years as a qualified family doctor. That's something, but I'd still be thirty-two with my thinking work gone. The hands-on side would last until about 2034, so I'd have a bit longer if I lean into it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my training first, no shortcuts. In the second year I'd add a diploma in minor surgery or women's health, where my hands matter. I'd keep the union work going, and we'd save hard and hold off on buying a flat until we see how it lands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but with something to do about it. That's better than the two-year one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about leaving medicine?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not leaving, but maybe changing which part I do. I always liked the hospice placement, sitting with people, and that's not something I'd hand to a machine even if it could do it. I'd look at palliative care seriously.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Jonas be doing in those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd be facing his own version at school. We talked once about one of us retraining while the other keeps a steady income. I think he'd go first, because his school is closer to the edge than my clinic.

say: I'd call it a **warning** we'd be fools to waste.
I'd want the health service **planning now** for what doctors do after AI diagnosis.
think: Five years lets me **finish training** and work a couple of years as a qualified doctor.
At thirty-two my **thinking work** would be gone, with hands-on work lasting to about 2034.
do: Add a **diploma** in minor surgery or women's health in year two.
Hold off **buying a flat** and save hard until the picture is clearer.
feel: **Worried**, but with a plan to work on, which feels better than two years.
S3.quote: I always liked the hospice placement, sitting with people, and that's not something I'd hand to a machine even if it could do it.
fieldNote: The extra three years turn **fear into a plan** for her.
She looks towards **palliative care**, where human presence matters most.
The couple would take **turns retraining**, with her partner's job seen as more at risk.
Still expects to lose her thinking work, so **anxious** rather than uneasy.

steps.text: Finish training, then take a minor surgery diploma in year two
Put the plan to buy a flat on hold
Keep pushing the union on health service planning
Save hard while her partner considers retraining first

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven when it arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do this properly, if governments actually use it. I'd push for health workers to have a seat at the table when the rules get written.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be okay, or at least not alone. By then I'd be an experienced family doctor, and the union would have had a decade to fight for retraining and fair pay. The hands-on part would carry me to about 2039, and maybe I'd have moved into palliative care by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish training, then spend a few years getting really good at the human parts: hard conversations, end-of-life care, procedures. I'd stand for a role on the union's health committee. And we'd probably buy a small flat after all, because ten years is too long to put life on hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I can breathe. It feels like weather coming rather than a wall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a medical student starting now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell a medical student to learn the parts patients would cry about losing, not the parts they'd happily skip. Nobody misses the waiting room. People miss the doctor who held their hand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does ten years change whether you'd have children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a little. Jonas and I want kids in a few years, and ten years of warning means I wouldn't panic about it. I'd just want a job that still exists when they start school.

say: I'd say **ten years** is enough to do this properly, if governments use it.
I'd push for **health workers** to have a seat when the rules are written.
think: By then I'd be an **experienced** doctor with a decade of union work behind me.
**Hands-on** work would carry me to about 2039, maybe in palliative care.
do: Finish training, then build skill in **hard conversations** and end-of-life care.
Buy a **small flat** rather than put life on hold.
feel: **Uneasy**, but able to breathe, like **weather coming** rather than a wall.
S4.quote: I'd tell a medical student to learn the parts patients would cry about losing, not the parts they'd happily skip.
fieldNote: The decade lets her see herself as **experienced**, not a junior to be replaced.
Her faith in **collective action** grows with the time available.
She'd go ahead with **family plans**, a sign of real reassurance.
Worry stays in the background, so **uneasy** rather than anxious.

steps.text: Build skill in end-of-life care after finishing training
Stand for a seat on the union's health committee
Buy a small flat with her partner within a few years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, by a mile, because I'd be caught halfway through training with nothing finished. What would help is a guaranteed training place and pay for junior doctors while the health service works out what our job becomes. And a real say for the people who work in clinics, not just the people selling software.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe who I'd blame. Not the technology, really, but owners and governments who'd use it to cut costs instead of shortening waiting lists. A machine that gives Eastgate more doctor time is a gift; one that gives us fewer doctors is a choice someone made.

headlineQuote: A machine that gives Eastgate more doctor time is a gift; one that gives us fewer doctors is a choice someone made.
portrait: A **27-year-old** junior family doctor at a publicly funded clinic in the poorest part of town.
She lives with her **teacher partner**, has about four months saved, and pays off a **student loan**.
She'll use **AI tools** once colleagues prove them, and leans on her **union** for change.
The **two-year** picture alarms her; with ten years she feels uneasy but able to plan.
She'd move towards **hands-on** procedures and palliative care, where people matter most.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she'd be caught halfway through training with nothing finished.
whatWouldHelp: A **guaranteed training place** and pay for junior doctors while the service adapts.
A real **say** for clinic workers, not just software sellers.
